paras: The Alexandria third-ward polling violence took place on November 2, 1880, when Black Republican voters waiting at the court-house polls in Alexandria, Virginia, were crowded out, beaten and clubbed, and one was stabbed. Republican papers and witnesses blamed Democratic 'roughs' and Mayor Cortland Smith's police, while the Alexandria Gazette denied that any intimidation occurred. Republicans cited the episode as evidence against claims of peaceful Southern elections and threatened to contest the seat of the winning Democratic congressman, Barbour.

Alexandria held a closely fought election for president and Congress, and Democrats had tried to disqualify Republicans who had paid their capitation tax to a disputed collector until the county judge allowed them to vote. According to a Washington correspondent, the city's roughly four hundred Black voters had paid the poll tax and met the state's requirements.

The Kenosha Telegraph's informants said some Black men voted without hindrance in the morning before the mayor arrived with a police force and told them to stand back and make room for white men. Those who did not obey readily were 'roughly handled, their clothes torn,' and some were injured, a treatment the letter said continued through the day. The National Republican's report instead described 'gangs of democratic roughs' repeatedly cutting into the line while the mayor, Chapman Neale and Alexander Hunter egged them on.

By about 3 o'clock it was clear not all could vote before sundown, and the mayor called out the whole police force, which formed separate lines of white and Black voters. After Major Burke urged Republicans to keep the peace and Neale told Democrats that 200 Black men had been sent to intimidate voters, a fight broke out that was 'with difficulty suppressed.' Men with double-barreled shotguns appeared in the crowd, a nearby fence was stripped of palings to arm the Democrats, and several Black men were seriously hurt, one stabbed in the side.

A. W. Harris wrote that he saw police club 'innocent and inoffensive colored men,' that a man was severely cut, and that a Democrat drew a revolver on him. About 100 voters, mostly Republicans, were still in line when the polls closed, though other counts of those shut out ran from two hundred to several hundred.

No arrest for the assaults appears in the coverage, and the fate of the stabbed man was not reported. On November 8 a meeting of Black Republicans in the third ward condemned the mayor and police for their conduct at the election. In January 1881 a federal grand jury indicted James Cole for obstructing voters at the third-ward polls, and in March a jury acquitted him of delaying a Black voter, Abner Anderson.

The Washington National Republican headlined its report 'Disgraceful Row at the Polls' and followed with an editorial saying the mayor and police drove voters 'like cattle from the ballot-box' with 'force and even bloodshed.' Gen. E. W. Whitaker repeated the charge in Washington speeches, and the Chicago Tribune and Evening Star relayed it as a report. A Washington letter in the Kenosha Telegraph used Alexandria to rebut talk of 'peaceable elections' in the South, calling the mayor and police 'a mob in official uniform.'

The Alexandria Gazette called the charges an 'imaginary outrage,' praised the police for keeping the peace, and blamed the crowding on Black men it said had been brought from Washington, using a slur. It called Whitaker's account false and mocked the Black Republicans' protest meeting as wanting 'a fuss for the party's sake.'

Accounts differ over who used force: the National Republican's news report blamed Democratic roughs, while Harris, Whitaker and the Kenosha correspondent blamed the police directly. The Gazette said the mayor only ordered spectators cleared to speed the voting, but it named no witnesses, whereas Harris wrote as a named eyewitness.

reader.title: Alexandria third-ward polling violence
bases: Black Republican voters at the third-ward polls were beaten, clubbed and one stabbed by Democratic 'roughs' and, in several accounts, by city police acting under the mayor (A6, A13, A17).

Several Republican sources describe force and injuries (A6, A13, A17, A7), while the Alexandria Gazette calls the charges of intimidation groundless and says the mayor only cleared spectators (A10, A12).

accounts.label: National Republican local report
accounts.gist: Democratic roughs repeatedly broke the voters' line with the mayor and party leaders egging them on; after Neale's speech a fight broke out, palings and shotguns appeared, several Black men were hurt and one stabbed.

accounts.label: Republican eyewitnesses (Harris, Whitaker, Kenosha correspondent)
accounts.gist: The mayor and police drove Black voters from the polls, clubbing them and ordering them to make room for white men.

accounts.label: Alexandria Gazette
accounts.gist: No intimidation occurred; the mayor cleared crowding spectators, the police kept the peace, and congestion was caused by Black men 'imported' from Washington.

framing.detail: The National Republican headlined 'Disgraceful Row at the Polls' and editorialized that the mayor and police drove voters 'like cattle' from the ballot-box.
The Kenosha Telegraph's Washington letter used Alexandria to rebut 'peaceable elections' in the South, calling the police 'a mob in official uniform'.
The Alexandria Gazette called the charges an 'imaginary outrage', praised the police and blamed Black Washingtonians, using a slur.
The Chicago Tribune and Evening Star relayed the charges as reports and speeches.
